Aggravate means to make something bad even worse, or in informal use, to annoy or irritate someone. Those are its two meanings, and both are widely accepted today.
Meaning 1 — To Make Something Worse (The Core, Formal Meaning)

This is the primary and most precise meaning of the word. When you aggravate something, you take a problem, condition, or situation that is already bad and push it to a more severe, more serious, or more intense state.

The key idea is: it was already bad. You made it worse.

Examples:

  • "Running on a broken leg will aggravate the injury." (The injury was already there. Running makes it more serious.)
  • "The drought was aggravated by people overusing water." (The drought existed. Overuse made it worse.)
  • "His rude comments aggravated the tension between the two groups." (Tension already existed. His words intensified it.)
  • "Skipping meals can aggravate the symptoms of diabetes." (The symptoms exist. Skipping meals pushes them to a worse state.)

What kinds of things can be aggravated?

Almost any bad thing can be aggravated — a disease, a wound, a conflict, a crisis, a problem, suffering, pain, poverty, or symptoms. As a rule of thumb: if it's unpleasant and already exists, it can be aggravated.

Synonyms for this meaning: worsen, intensify, exacerbate, compound, deepen, heighten, inflame.
Meaning 2 — To Annoy or Irritate a Person (The Informal Meaning)

In everyday speech, people also use aggravate to mean to irritate, bother, or get on someone's nerves. In this sense, the "something bad" is not a situation — it's a person's emotional state.

Examples:

  • "Stop tapping your pen. You're aggravating me." (You are irritating me.)
  • "The slow internet connection really aggravates her when she's trying to work."
  • "Nothing aggravates him more than people being late."
  • "Her constant interruptions were deeply aggravating."

Synonyms for this meaning: irritate, annoy, bother, exasperate, frustrate, vex, get on someone's nerves.
A Note on the Two Meanings (Important!)

There is a long-running debate about Meaning 2. Traditional grammar purists argue that aggravate should only mean "to make something worse" and that using it to mean "to annoy" is incorrect. According to them, if you want to say someone is annoying you, you should say irritate or annoy instead.

However, modern dictionaries — including Merriam-Webster and Oxford — fully accept both meanings. The "to annoy" sense has been in common use for centuries and is widely understood. In formal or professional writing (legal documents, medical reports, academic papers), stick to Meaning 1. In everyday conversation and informal writing, both meanings are perfectly fine.

The bottom line: know your audience. In a doctor's report or a business document, use it to mean "make worse." In casual speech, both meanings work.

When used as an adjective, aggravated can describe:

1. A person who feels annoyed:
"She had an aggravated look on her face." (She looked irritated/frustrated.)

2. Something made worse:
"Aggravated symptoms kept him in the hospital longer."

3. A legal term — Aggravated [crime]:
In law, "aggravated" means a crime was committed with additional factors that make it more severe. For example:

  • Aggravated assault = an assault made more serious because a weapon was used, or the victim was especially vulnerable.
  • Aggravated theft = theft made more serious due to factors like violence involved.

The word "aggravated" in law essentially means: "not just [the crime], but a worse, more serious version of it."

FormExample
Aggravate (verb)"Don't aggravate the wound."
Aggravated (past tense / adjective)"He aggravated his back injury." / "She felt aggravated."
Aggravating (present participle / adjective)"The noise is aggravating the situation." / "What an aggravating habit!"
Aggravation (noun)"The project caused him endless aggravation." (meaning: irritation or added trouble)
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Irritate — Can mean both "to annoy a person" AND "to make a body part sore/inflamed" (e.g., "The soap irritated her skin."). It overlaps with aggravate in both meanings but is slightly more about surface-level discomfort or mild annoyance.
  • Exacerbate — Means exactly the same as Meaning 1 of aggravate (to make worse), but it is more formal and academic. You'd see it in medical or academic writing more than in everyday conversation.
  • Provoke — This means to deliberately stir up a reaction or emotion in someone. Aggravating someone can be unintentional; provoking is usually intentional.

• Aggravate = make something bad even worse (the core, always-correct meaning)
  • Aggravate = annoy or irritate someone (informal, but widely accepted)
  • In formal/professional contexts, use it only for Meaning 1.
  • The noun form is aggravation, the adjective is aggravating or aggravated.
  • In law, aggravated means a more serious version of a crime.

The easiest way to remember it: think of the word "grave" sitting inside ag-grave-ate. A grave situation is serious. To aggravate is to make it even more grave — more serious, more severe, more intense. That image captures the heart of the word perfectly.
